analysis.one_liner: Bans agreements between employers not to hire or recruit each other's workers.
analysis.headline: The bill to outlaw employer no-poach agreements never got a committee vote or a House floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The End Employer Collusion Act would make it illegal for two or more employers to agree — directly, through a franchise deal, or through a contractor-subcontractor deal — not to solicit or hire each other's current or former employees. These 'no-poach' agreements can hold down wages by keeping workers from getting competing job offers. The bill would let workers sue for damages and would put the Federal Trade Commission in charge of enforcement, the same way it polices other unfair competition.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies that use no-poach or no-solicitation agreements, especially fast-food and franchise workers, low-wage hourly staff, and employees of large chains where such pacts are common. If the ban were in effect, competing employers could bid for their labor, which tends to raise wages and widen job options.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at chains using no-poach pacts

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for any employer to enter into, enforce, or threaten to enforce an agreement with another employer that prohibits or restricts hiring or soliciting that other employer's employees or former employees, including agreements embedded in franchise or contractor-subcontractor deals [S2].
Any individual harmed by such an agreement could sue in federal court for actual damages plus punitive damages, plus attorney's fees and costs if they win [S2].
The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the ban with the same powers it has under the Federal Trade Commission Act, adding a government enforcement path alongside private lawsuits [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that currently use no-poach or no-solicitation agreements — notably franchise chains, franchisors, and companies that coordinate hiring with contractors or staffing firms — would give up those agreements and face damage awards and FTC enforcement. Some economists and employers argue such clauses sometimes serve legitimate purposes, like protecting training investments, and those uses would be swept up too.

drawbacks.text: The bill bans all restrictive employment agreements between employers outright, with no exception for cases where a clause protects a legitimate business interest — for example, a contractor whose employees are embedded at a client company, where a no-hire clause is how staffing arrangements work [S2].

Because the definition reaches agreements 'through a franchise agreement or a contractor-subcontractor agreement,' ordinary commercial relationships could generate private lawsuits for actual and punitive damages, raising litigation risk for franchisors and subcontractors [S2].

The FTC already treats no-poach agreements as potentially illegal unfair methods of competition under existing law, so the bill partly adds a private right of action on top of enforcement authority that already exists, rather than closing a total gap [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: no-poach agreements are widely understood to suppress wages by removing competition for workers, and the bill's private right of action would give individual workers a way to fight back that current antitrust law largely does not. The cost is that the bill is written as a flat ban with no rule-of-reason carve-out, so it could also reach ordinary staffing, subcontracting, and franchise arrangements where a limited no-hire clause is how the deal works, creating litigation exposure. A narrower draft with an exception for legitimate business purposes would have carried less risk to the same goal.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to three House committees, but none of them ever took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill with Rep. Lou Correa on July 26, 2023 [S1][S2].

The Speaker referred it to the Education and Workforce, Energy and Commerce, and Judiciary Committees, and days later the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce got a referral [S4].
No committee held a markup, no subcommittee held a hearing, and the bill never received a vote in the House or Senate before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on no-poach and no-solicitation agreements — franchise chains, franchisors, and firms that coordinate hiring with contractors — are better off, since the ban never took effect and their existing agreements remain lawful except where the FTC or antitrust enforcers act separately.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only two House supporters were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored it and no recorded vote or stated opposition exists, so the partisan shape is undefined beyond the sponsorship.

industries.note: No-poach and no-solicitation clauses are common in franchise systems, holding workers in place across franchised locations. The bill would make those clauses unlawful and expose franchisors to damages suits.

industries.industry: Large employers using inter-firm no-poach agreements
industries.note: Companies that informally or formally agree not to recruit each other's staff would lose a tool that keeps wages down by limiting competing offers, and could face FTC penalties and private suits.

Contractor-subcontractor no-hire clauses are often how staffing placements are protected, so the flat ban reaches some legitimate commercial arrangements even as it frees their placed workers to accept better jobs.

industries.industry: Workers represented by employment litigation (plaintiffs' bar)
industries.note: The bill creates a private right of action with attorney's fees and punitive damages, generating a new avenue for workers to sue over restrictive employment agreements.
